To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
APPL1 regulates PI3K-dependent synaptic plasticity, which is a form of synaptic plasticity that is independent from PDK1/Akt activation.
the adaptor protein containing a PH domain, PTB domain and leucin-zipper motif 1 (APP1) gates the activation of the PI3K pathway at the plasma membrane during synaptic plasticity.
APPL1 regulates synaptic plasticity by gating PI3K-dependent events, but not by regulating PDK1 and/or Akt.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that control synaptic plasticity in hippocampal neurons.
how the endosomal trafficking machinery is integrated into synaptic plasticity events.
how synaptic activity is converted into changes in the postsynaptic density, which are the basis of memory storage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
APPL1 regulates the PI3K pathway at the membrane level, but the downstream effectors of this pathway are not Akt and PDK1.
APPL1 acts as a ‘gatekeeper’ of the PI3K pathway at the plasma membrane during LTP induction.
APPL1 acts as a molecular gate that controls the access to PI3K signaling in the plasma membrane, thus determining the synaptic plasticity outcome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
APPL1 acts as a molecular gate for the PI3K pathway at the plasma membrane, and that this pathway is differentially engaged in different forms of plasticity.
APPL1 acts as a gatekeeper for the PIP3 pathway at the plasma membrane, and that this is crucial for the induction of LTP, but not mGluR-LTP.
APPL1 acts as a gate for the activation of PI3K-dependent signaling cascades upon LTP induction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
APPL1 acts as a molecular gate to PI3K signaling, which is essential to the expression of LTP and mGluR-LTP.
the PI3K pathway is gated by APPL1, which acts as an adaptor protein at the plasma membrane to recruit PI3K and activate it.
the same protein can gate different synaptic plasticity events, depending on the signaling pathway involved.
